title: Mutal Poruḷ
paragraphs: Darwin’s theory has succeeded in scientifically explaining the human being’s evolution from the monkey. Among this teeming sea of humanity, growing in their multitudes, owing to diversification development and witnessed in this world, somewhere around five thousand years ago, the Tamil race was gradually preparing itself for a systematic form of life.

Leading an unorganized life is poles apart from leading a planned course of living. In order to formulate such a structured life, communication tools are mandatory. Among these communication tools, language has stood the test of time and stands as numero uno.

The races emerging from various parts of the world had been using their languages, but the Tamil race has had the distinction of standardizing its language and developing literature and grammar at a very early stage. The historically renowned Tamil race is credited with providing sheen and glitter to their language two thousand years ago, though the development process itself started some three thousand years earlier.

Tolkāppiyam’s Poruḷatikāram section, the grammar of literature and life, is a perfect telltale example of that feat. Though the modes of living and patterns of behaviour mentioned in Tolkāppiyam were very much in practice much before the Tolkāppiyam’s era, we can always recollect with pride that the arduous task of piecing them together and presenting them in the form of a poetic garland was effortlessly accomplished by Tolkāppiyar.
It may be debatable as to how many of the principles, beliefs and practices of
that era are relevant to the contemporary milieu. But there is no denying the fact that we would be woefully missing the mirrors of the past in the absence of landmark books like Tolkāppiyam.
In this context and background, let’s enjoy a few of the blossoms from the Poruḷatikāram section of Tolkāppiyam.
Of the three components of structure and content in literature, mutal poruḷ, karupporuḷ and uripporuḷ, mutal poruḷ has been divided into two, viz., land and time.
> Mutalporuḷ is > Aspects of land and time, > So do men of discernment find. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 4)

The land has been classified into pastoral tract (mullai), hilly tract (kuṟiñci), agricultural tract (marutam) and maritime tract (neytal). Each one of them has been assigned a presiding deity. And these deities supposedly protected and blessed the respective divisions of the Tamil land. Here is the Tolkāppiyam verse:

> The forest tract which Māyōṉ tends, > The hilly tract which Cēyōṉ tends > The fertile cultivable tract which Vēntaṉ tends > And the littoral tract which Varuṇaṉ tends > Are known to be > Mullai, kuṟiñci, marutam and neytal respectively. > > (Poruḷatikāram : Akattiṇai iyal, verse 5)
\*Gods equated with Tirumāl, Murukaṉ, Intiraṉ and Varuṇaṉ respectively by the commentators.
